label: Dual Affine Connections
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 131 to 161, asks how one Riemannian metric can support two different notions of straightness. The pairing of a primal and a dual affine connection through that metric is the structural seed for every dually flat manifold, divergence, and projection theorem we will meet.

label: One Metric, Two Connections
notes: A dual pair of connections satisfies a compatibility law: differentiating an inner product splits cleanly when the two vectors are transported by opposite connections. Neither connection need be metric on its own; together they preserve the metric, which is the defining algebraic balance of the entire dual geometry.

label: Dual Coordinate Systems
notes: A dually flat manifold carries two affine charts. The theta coordinates are flat for the primal connection, the eta coordinates are flat for the dual connection. Each chart has straight coordinate lines, and the two grids are biorthogonal, meaning their basis vectors pair to the identity under the metric.

label: Convex Potentials and Legendre
notes: A convex potential psi of theta generates the dual coordinates by its gradient, eta equals grad psi. The Legendre transform produces a second convex potential phi of eta whose gradient inverts the map. The two potentials are tied by a single scalar identity that drives the canonical divergence.

label: Canonical Divergence
notes: The canonical divergence is the Bregman gap between the potential surface and its supporting tangent plane. It is nonnegative, vanishes exactly on the diagonal, and is generally asymmetric. For a Bernoulli model it equals the reversed Kullback-Leibler divergence, which the notebook verifies to ten decimal places.

label: Bregman Gap Geometry
notes: Reading the divergence as a vertical gap below the tangent line makes its three core properties visible at once. Convexity of psi forces the gap to be nonnegative, tangency forces it to vanish at the contact point, and curvature away from contact produces the asymmetry between the two orientations.

label: Mixed Coordinates
notes: Mixed coordinates splice the two charts, holding some components in eta and the rest in theta. A primal-flat sheet and a dual-flat sheet then meet at a single point that behaves like an orthogonal projection. This splice is the coordinate machinery that exposes the Pythagorean decomposition.

label: Generalized Pythagorean Theorem
notes: When the dual geodesic from P to R meets the primal geodesic from R to Q orthogonally, the canonical divergence splits additively, exactly like a squared Euclidean distance. The notebook confirms the residual is zero to twelve decimals on a product Bernoulli model, even though the geometry is curved.

label: Dual Geodesic Projection
notes: Projecting a point onto a flat submanifold means following a dual geodesic until it meets the surface at a right angle. The Pythagorean theorem guarantees this foot is the unique divergence minimizer, which is the geometric engine behind maximum likelihood and the cut computations that follow.

label: k-Cuts as Forced Factorization
notes: A k-cut replaces a coupled distribution by the nearest member of a lower-interaction family, deleting coupling across a partition. That nearest member is a dual projection, and the canonical divergence to it measures the interaction the cut cannot express. Finer partitions lose more, so divergence ranks them.

label: Applied Lab: Integrated Information
notes: The lab compares a two-node binary Markov kernel with a cut kernel that predicts each node from only its own present state. The averaged divergence is a phi-like measure of irreducible structure. As cross-node coupling rises, that lost predictive information grows monotonically, confirming the projection picture numerically.

label: Pitfalls and Recap
notes: Remember that dual connections share one metric and are never independent geometries, that a flat chart is not Euclidean, and that divergence orientation matters. Mixed coordinates only yield Pythagoras when submanifolds meet orthogonally in the dual sense. Cuts are projections; their leftover divergence is the lesson.
